verdicts.question: What type of roof is present at the site?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10, 11, 12 and 15: the rooftop photos show a flat concrete terrace with red waterproof coating, parapet edges and no slope. The site model on pages 5-6 also shows flat roof slabs.
verdicts.rationale: The flat red-coated RCC terrace is clearly visible in several roof photos, which matches 'RCC Flat Roof'.

verdicts.question: Are there any obstructions on the roof that could affect the solar installation?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10, 12 and 15: there are 4-5 satellite dish antennas with masts and loose cables inside the 'Proposed PV area' / 'PV modules' overlay. A black polythene-covered object and an adjacent sloped translucent roof are also visible. Pages 11 and 16 show a cluster of about 9 water tanks on the next terrace. Page 18 Customer Scope #4 says the existing dish antennas must be removed or relocated before installation.
verdicts.rationale: The designer answered 'No' obstructions, but the photos show dish antennas sitting inside the proposed array footprint, and the report's own Customer Scope requires them to be removed or relocated. That is a clear contradiction. The 2 m elevated structure may clear the tanks and parapet, but the antennas are a real obstruction.

verdicts.question: What is the angle of the panels? (in degrees)
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 5-7: the 3D structure models show a 2P4 elevated array with a modest single tilt. The front and rear legs differ only slightly in height, which looks like roughly 10°. No measured angle annotation is given (only the 2.00 m clearance).
verdicts.rationale: The low tilt in the renders is consistent with 10°. There is no photo of the actual angle, so this is a visual estimate only.

verdicts.question: On how many roofs at the site are we installing solar?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 5-6 and 12: one array of 8 modules (2P4) is placed on a single upper roof slab. Only one 'Proposed PV area' is marked.
verdicts.rationale: A single roof area is shown in both the layout and the photos, matching '1'.

verdicts.question: What type of mounting structure is planned?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 7: '2P4 structure with 2m height' render shows tall column legs with base plates, purlins and rafters, i.e. an elevated structure. Pages 5-6 show the array raised above the terrace and tanks.
verdicts.rationale: An elevated structure is clearly shown. The HDGI material/finish can't be confirmed from renders, but the structure type matches.

verdicts.question: What is the orientation of the solar panels?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 5: the plan view has a north arrow pointing up the page with the array placed centrally. The 3D renders show the panel tilt, but the facing direction relative to the north arrow can't be confirmed reliably at this resolution. The site photos have no compass cue.
verdicts.rationale: Orientation can't be confirmed for certain from the renders or photos. Check the tilt direction against the north arrow in the SketchUp model.

verdicts.question: How can the roof be accessed?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10 and 13: a tall aluminium extension ladder is propped against the wall to reach the upper roof slab (headroom top), where the PV is proposed. The page 5 render also shows a ladder on the roof. Lower floors are reached by the internal staircase (pages 9, 11).
verdicts.rationale: The ladder to the PV roof level is clearly visible, matching 'Ladder'.

verdicts.question: Is the building currently under construction?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 8: the building exterior shows a finished apartment block with cladding, glass balconies and a finished entrance. Pages 9 and 11 show finished staircases with railings.
verdicts.rationale: The building is clearly finished and occupied, not under construction.

verdicts.question: In an under-construction building, are existing conduit pipes available for AC, DC cables, and earthing?
verdicts.photo_observation: The building is not under construction (see roof Q11), so this question doesn't really apply. Page 17 shows an existing service shaft with cables and pipes, which the routing plan uses.
verdicts.rationale: This applies only to under-construction buildings. The designer's 'No' is moot. An existing duct shaft is visible on page 17.

verdicts.question: What is the height of the building and how many floors does it have?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 8: the building exterior shows a multi-storey residential block with several balcony levels above the ground entrance, but a tree trunk and canopy hide much of the facade and the top floors. Floors and height can't be counted reliably.
verdicts.rationale: A multi-storey building is visible, but trees hide the floor count. G+4 / 18 m can't be confirmed from the photo.

verdicts.question: Is the site photo matching with the building description?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 8: the building exterior photo shows a multi-storey apartment block ('ESCALA PARKVIEW'). The rooftop photos (pages 10-12) show a high vantage point over the surrounding buildings, consistent with an upper-floor terrace.
verdicts.rationale: The site photo is consistent with a multi-storey residential building as described.

verdicts.question: Is there an overhead HT line passing within a 10-meter radius of the site?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10, 12 and 15: the rooftop panoramas show surrounding buildings, trees and sky. Only thin dish/TV cables and a light cord are visible. No overhead HT conductors or towers can be seen near the roof.
verdicts.rationale: No HT lines are visible in the wide rooftop photos. Ground-level street wiring isn't fully covered.

verdicts.question: Can the delivery van/truck reach the material unloading point?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 8, Building Exterior / Material Delivery Route: the building entrance faces a paved road/forecourt with motorbikes parked. The blue delivery route starts at the road edge and goes up the entrance steps.
verdicts.rationale: The road-front entrance is accessible for an unloading vehicle. The road width isn't fully shown.

verdicts.question: Are there any obstacles at the site that could hinder material lifting?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 8-11 and 13, delivery route: entrance steps, then an internal dog-leg staircase with tight 180° turns and handrails (page 9). The staircase is annotated as about 1 m wide (page 11). The final level is reached by a vertical extension ladder (pages 10, 13). The modules are 2382 x 1134 mm (page 1).
verdicts.rationale: Moving 2.38 m modules through a 1 m dog-leg staircase and then up a ladder could be a lifting constraint, despite the 'No' answer. This isn't a clear contradiction, but it needs a reviewer's check (rope hoisting or another lifting method may be needed).

verdicts.question: Where will the Inverter, DCDB, ACDB, Battery, etc. be located?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: an indoor room below the roof is annotated with Inverter, Battery and UPS point boxes on the wall, with DC cable entering from the roof opening. Page 14 shows the solar meter proposed on a wall column next to the LT panel and the main meter in the LT panel.
verdicts.rationale: The designer's answer is blank ('-'), but the photos do show a proposed equipment location (an indoor wall room near the roof). The written answer needs to be filled in. ACDB/DCDB positions aren't explicitly marked.

verdicts.question: Is a canopy required for protecting the Inverters/ACDB/DCDB?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: the inverter/battery location is inside a room with a ceiling and walls. Part of one side has a black-sheet-covered opening.
verdicts.rationale: The equipment is in a sheltered indoor room, so a canopy isn't needed, which matches 'No'. Weather exposure through the sheet-covered opening should be noted.

verdicts.question: Did you discuss the location of the earth pits with the customer?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 16: a ground/basement utility area has a wall labelled 'Earth Point', with the earthing cable route marked down to it. Page 17 caption: customer to run 6 sq.mm copper through conduit up to the earthing location.
verdicts.rationale: The earth point location on the ground level is marked in the photos, consistent with 'Yes, on ground floor'.

verdicts.question: Where is the Internet Router located?
verdicts.photo_observation: No photo of the internet router or its location is included in pages 4-17.
verdicts.rationale: Can't be verified visually.

verdicts.question: What's the Wi-Fi strength of the router near to the String inverter/Envoy?
verdicts.photo_observation: No Wi-Fi signal-strength evidence (screenshot or router photo) is included. Page 18 Customer Scope says 'WIFI upto inverter location' is the customer's responsibility.
verdicts.rationale: Can't be verified visually. The customer-scope note suggests Wi-Fi at the inverter isn't yet guaranteed.

verdicts.question: Did you pin the site location in your WhatsApp when you were at the site?
verdicts.photo_observation: This isn't a photo item. Page 1 lists GPS coordinates 12.8961, 77.5957 and a Google Maps link. A WhatsApp pin isn't visible in the report.
verdicts.rationale: GPS coordinates are in the report, but the WhatsApp pin can't be verified from the photos.

verdicts.question: What type of energy meter is currently installed?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 15 (zoomed): a small polycarbonate-cased electronic meter with an LCD showing 'Ph.. kW 0.00', a single scroll button, a single green indicator, and one porcelain kit-kat cut-out fuse beside it. This is the typical BESCOM single-phase static meter. Another similar meter is visible below.
verdicts.rationale: The meter is clearly a digital single-phase meter.

verdicts.question: Is the Meter cubicle photo matching with the previous answer?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 15 shows the meter cubicle with a single-phase digital meter, consistent with electrical Q1.
verdicts.rationale: The cubicle photo matches 'Single-phase, Digital'.

verdicts.question: Has the termination point in the Main meter panel been identified?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 14: the LT meter panel photo has the 'Main meter' cubicle highlighted in red, with the AC cable route (purple) drawn into it.
verdicts.rationale: The termination cubicle is clearly marked in the main meter panel.

verdicts.question: Is the Termination Point easily visible or sealed?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 14-15: the meter compartments in the multi-tenant LT panel are behind closed (likely sealed) doors. Page 15 shows the meter visible with the door open. The termination terminals aren't clearly shown.
verdicts.rationale: The meter is visible, but whether the termination point is easily accessible or sealed by BESCOM can't be confirmed from the photos.

verdicts.question: Is a Lightning Arrestor (LA) already available at the site?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10, 12 and 15: the rooftop photos show no existing lightning arrestor spike or down-conductor. Page 15 marks a new LA (yellow dot) at the array corner, and page 7 shows 'LA extension required'.
verdicts.rationale: No existing LA is visible, and a new LA is proposed, which matches 'No'.

verdicts.question: In Main meter panel, is empty space available for solar meter?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 14: the LT panel is fully populated with meter/MCCB compartments. The solar meter is proposed outside the panel on the adjacent wall column (blue 'Solar meter' box).
verdicts.rationale: Placing the solar meter outside the panel is consistent with 'No' empty space in the main meter panel.

verdicts.question: Is there space available to dig DC, AC and LA earth pits?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 16 shows a ground-level utility area with an 'Earth Point' label and existing pipes. Page 17 caption says the customer will run copper through conduit to the earthing location. No open soil area for new DC/AC/LA pits is clearly photographed.
verdicts.rationale: Space for three new earth pits isn't clearly shown. The photos suggest connection to an existing earth point rather than new pits.

verdicts.question: What type of Earthing chamber needs to be installed at site? Is it Cement chamber or PVC chamber?
verdicts.photo_observation: No photo of a proposed earthing chamber or pit location showing chamber type.
verdicts.rationale: The chamber type can't be verified visually.

verdicts.question: In case of elevated structures, is an LA extension provided at the far end?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 7: the render captioned 'LA extension required' shows an LA extension arm at the far corner of the elevated structure. The LA is also marked on page 15.
verdicts.rationale: The LA extension is clearly shown in the structure drawing.

verdicts.question: In case of elevated structures, is it with or without grouting?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 7: the structure render shows legs with base plates on the slab. Grouting or pedestal blocks aren't depicted. The text checklist notes a concrete depth of 200 mm.
verdicts.rationale: The base plates are visible, but grouting isn't explicitly shown. It is only implied by the 200 mm concrete note.

verdicts.question: Are there any challenges with respect to Installation and Maintenance activities?
verdicts.photo_observation: The photos show dish antennas inside the PV footprint that need relocating (pages 12, 15; Customer Scope #4), ladder-only access to the PV roof (pages 10, 13), a crowded water-tank terrace (pages 11, 16), and an equipment room far from the LT panel.
verdicts.rationale: Several installation/maintenance considerations are visible (antenna relocation, ladder access), which is at odds with 'No challenges'. A reviewer should confirm.

verdicts.question: Are there any safety risks associated with accessing the roof for installation?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10 and 13: the PV roof is reached by a single tall extension ladder about 18 m above ground. Page 12: the upper roof has a low parapet next to a sloped translucent sheet roof.
verdicts.rationale: Ladder-only access to a high roof with a low parapet and an adjacent fragile sheet roof may be a safety risk, despite the 'No' answer. A reviewer should judge it.

verdicts.question: Is space present in rooftop to store the panels?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 11, Material Storage: an open red-coated terrace floor between the water tanks, with enough clear area to lay modules flat.
verdicts.rationale: The storage space shown supports storing panels flat (horizontally).

verdicts.question: Is ventilation available in the battery location?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: the inverter/battery room has a large opening on the left (partly covered with black plastic sheet) and a window/vent on the upper wall.
verdicts.rationale: An opening is present, but it is partly covered. Whether there is adequate ventilation for the battery is unclear.

verdicts.question: Is Battery wall mounted or stand mounted?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: the 'Battery' box is annotated on the wall beside the inverter, at mid-wall height.
verdicts.rationale: The annotation shows a wall-mounted battery position, matching the answer.

verdicts.question: Should the Inverters/ACDB/DCDB be installed on a metal grill or wall mount?
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: the 'Inverter' box is annotated on the plastered wall, with no metal grill visible.
verdicts.rationale: The equipment location is on a solid wall, matching 'Wall mount'.

verdicts.question: Provide the dimensions for solar meter cubicle placement (L x W of wall).
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 14: the solar meter is proposed on a narrow plastered wall column/pilaster next to the LT panel. The column looks only about 300-450 mm wide compared with the panel modules.
verdicts.rationale: The marked column looks narrower than the stated 1000 mm width. A reviewer should verify the dimensions on site.

verdicts.question: Provide the dimension for earth pits location (L x W of available space).
verdicts.photo_observation: No photo shows the earth pit area with dimensions or a measuring reference. Page 16 shows only the 'Earth Point' wall.
verdicts.rationale: The earth pit area dimensions can't be verified visually.

verdicts.question: Is LAN cable under customer scope?
verdicts.photo_observation: No photo evidence for LAN. Page 18 Customer Scope lists 'WIFI upto inverter location' but no LAN item.
verdicts.rationale: Not verifiable from photos. The Customer Scope doesn't mention LAN, which is consistent with 'No'.

verdicts.question: Is there any shadow that affects the solar installation?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 10, 12 and 15: the proposed upper roof is open to the sky with no adjacent tall structure directly south. A taller neighbouring building and trees are visible to one side (page 10 lower, page 12 lower right). Dish antennas sit inside the footprint, and the 2 m elevated structure lifts the modules above the parapet and antennas. No shadow analysis is included.
verdicts.rationale: Shading looks limited thanks to the 2 m elevation, but there is a taller adjacent building and no shadow analysis to confirm. A reviewer should check.

verdicts.question: Is there any trench work to be done to carry the AC cable to the meter location?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 13, 14 and 17: the AC/earthing route runs inside the building, from the roof opening to the equipment room, down the internal service shaft (page 17), to the LT panel room (page 14). There is no external ground run.
verdicts.rationale: The routing is through an internal duct shaft, so no trenching is needed, consistent with 'No'.

verdicts.question: Is the cable routing in the site photos continuous and consistent across the documented run — from rooftop panels to DCDB to inverter to ACDB to solar meter to main panel — with no orphan ends, no unexplained mid-run size changes, and visible conduit / cable-tie / clipping where the run is exposed?
verdicts.designer_notes: No designer answer for this target — the vision routine verifies it by tracing cables across photos with 'Cable Routing', 'Equipment Location', 'Meter Box' and similar captions on pages 4+.
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 12: the DC route (red) goes from the PV modules across the roof to the roof edge. Page 13: the DC cable drops through the roof opening into the equipment room, to the Inverter, then the Battery, and the AC goes to the UPS point. Page 14: the AC (purple) enters the LT panel from above to the main meter, and the solar meter sits on the adjacent column. Pages 15-17: earthing (green/orange) goes along the parapet, down the service shaft to the ground 'Earth Point', with the cable size change (16 sq.mm Al to 6 sq.mm Cu) explained in the caption. Gaps: the AC run from the equipment room down several floors to the LT panel isn't photographed, the DCDB/ACDB aren't marked, and conduit/clipping on the exposed roof run isn't shown.
verdicts.rationale: The routing is mostly continuous and the earthing size change is explained, but the inverter-to-LT-panel AC segment and the DCDB/ACDB positions are missing, so continuity can't be fully confirmed.
